answer.label: Not Lao Tzu — a modern misattribution
answer.authorDates: trad. 6th century BC · legendary founder of Taoism, to whom the line is wrongly credited
answer.sourceLine: This sentence is not in the ‘Tao Te Ching’ or any authentic Laozi text, and love in this romantic sense is simply not a theme he treated. Its earliest documented appearance is in the American novelist Dean Koontz’s 1988 thriller ‘Lightning’ ↗, where Koontz himself pinned it on Lao Tzu — giving no source. Who first composed the line remains unknown; it reads as a modern, greeting-card sentiment, not a 6th-century-BC Chinese aphorism.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from
source.excerpt: Being deeply loved by someone gives you strength, while loving someone deeply gives you courage.
trail: The Taoism reference site taoistic.com ↗ flatly states “This is NOT a quote from Tao Te Ching,” noting love is not a subject Lao Tzu explored, and identifies the oldest book it can find the line in as Dean Koontz’s 1988 novel ‘Lightning.’
Wikiquote lists the line under ‘Misattributed’ ↗, giving the same earliest trace: ‘Lightning’ by Dean Koontz, 1988, who credited Lao Tzu and gave no source.
Goodreads carries the quote under Lao Tzu ↗ but flags it with a “widely-misattributed” tag.
No line of the ‘Tao Te Ching’ — searchable in full at Project Gutenberg ↗ — matches this sentiment.
source.excerptNote: A widely circulated swapped variant also exists — “To love someone deeply gives you strength; being loved by someone deeply gives you courage” — another sign of an unanchored, folk-transmitted line rather than a fixed translated text.
source.rightsNote: Because the true author of the exact wording is unknown — its earliest documented appearance is merely a 1988 novel that itself credited Lao Tzu — no copyright status can be responsibly asserted for the sentence. The Tao Te Ching and its old translations are long in the public domain, but this line is not from that work.

author.name: Lao Tzu
author.heading: About Lao Tzu
author.metaLine: trad. 6th century BC · legendary Chinese sage, reputed author of the Tao Te Ching
author.bio: Lao Tzu (Laozi) is the semi-legendary Chinese philosopher traditionally regarded as the founder of Taoism and author of the Tao Te Ching, a foundational text of some 81 short chapters. Its themes are the Tao (“the Way”), wu wei (effortless action), humility, and harmony with nature — not romantic love, which makes sentimental “love” lines like this one especially easy to spot as later inventions. Modern scholars doubt he was a single historical individual at all.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in Dean Koontz, ‘Lightning’ (New York: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1988), where the line is credited to Lao Tzu without a source; not present in the ‘Tao Te Ching.’ See also Wikiquote, “Laozi — Misattributed.”

misattribution.heading: How Lao Tzu got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most durable fake Lao Tzu lines — feel-good, quotable, and welded to a name that lends instant ancient authority.

items.who: Not in the Tao Te Ching
items.why: The Taoism reference site taoistic.com states plainly that this is not a quote from the Tao Te Ching ↗, observing that romantic love is not a subject Lao Tzu explored and that the phrasing reads like modern pop lyric rather than ancient aphorism.

The oldest book either Wikiquote ↗ or taoistic.com can find the line in is Koontz’s novel ‘Lightning’ (1988), where Koontz himself attributes it to Lao Tzu and cites no source — so even the earliest known appearance is a second-hand misattribution, not an original claim of authorship.
Sites such as BrainyQuote, Goodreads and countless graphics reprint it under Lao Tzu; Goodreads at least flags it ‘widely-misattributed’ ↗, but most reprints do not.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: not Lao Tzu. The line is absent from the ‘Tao Te Ching’, its author is unknown, and its earliest documented appearance is a 1988 Dean Koontz novel that already credited Lao Tzu without a source ↗.

context.heading: Why the misattribution sticks
lead: The sentiment is genuinely appealing — a neat chiasmus about how being loved and loving each grant a different gift. That symmetry is exactly what makes it memorable, and memorable lines drift toward famous names. Lao Tzu, remote and revered, is a magnet for any aphorism that sounds calm and wise.

But the ‘Tao Te Ching’ is a short, fully translated, endlessly searchable text, and this sentence is simply not in it. When even the earliest printed appearance — a 1988 thriller — is already handing the credit to Lao Tzu without a citation, the trail runs cold at a modern invention, not an ancient source.
context.pull: A memorable line drifts toward a famous name — and Lao Tzu is one of the strongest magnets there is.
